articles.title: The Nazis came to Kursk for history’s greatest tank victory. They found history’s greatest defense
articles.body:
The Nazis came to Kursk for history’s greatest tank victory. They found history’s greatest defense
By 1943, World War II had turned decisively in the Allies’ favor. At Stalingrad, the Russians destroyed the Wehrmacht’s largest field formation, the Sixth Army. In the Pacific, the Americans and their allies won a hard-fought victory over the Japanese at Guadalcanal. In North Africa, Allied forces trapped the German Afrika Korps and its Italian partners and forced them to surrender. And back in Russia, the Red Army won the decisive Battle of Kursk.
Beating the enemy with a shovel
In the winter of 1942-43, riding the momentum of their triumph at Stalingrad, Soviet forces launched a series of operations across the southern sector of their enormous front. Most met with at least some success. But in March, Field Marshal Erich von Manstein mounted a surprise counteroffensive that drove the Red Army’s battle-weary forces back from Kharkov and Belgorod.
Elsewhere, however, victory at Voronezh allowed the Russians to break through quickly to Kursk, a major transportation hub in central Russia. The result was a bulge in the front known in the West as the Kursk salient and in Russian as the Kurskaya Duga, or Kursk Arc. It projected roughly 150 kilometers westward, measured about 200 kilometers across at its base, and had Kursk at its center. To the north, it was flanked by the German-held Orel salient, which was roughly the same size. To the south, the German line formed a right angle with Belgorod at its corner.
The broad outline of Germany’s plan for the summer campaign of 1943 practically drew itself. After a winter of brutal fighting, the Wehrmacht no longer had enough strength to attack in several directions at once. Kursk, however, offered the best possible target for one concentrated blow. Major highway and rail hubs to the north at Orel and to the south at Belgorod and Kharkov would ease the logistical burden. The attack would have to cover a relatively modest distance – about 100 kilometers from each direction. By comparison, the Germans had advanced as much as 500 kilometers during their drive on Stalingrad in the summer of 1942. Encircling the Soviet armies inside the salient would inflict losses so severe that, for the next several months – perhaps even for the rest of the war – the Russians would be reduced to simply holding the line.
The coming operation was code-named Citadel. German forces would strike along converging axes at the base of the Kursk salient, then surge into the rear of the Soviet armies deployed inside it.
At first, the Germans did not intend to wait long. They planned to launch the offensive in the spring of 1943. Then other considerations intervened. In their memoirs, German generals usually had an elegant way of assigning responsibility for controversial decisions to a dead Führer who could no longer answer back. In reality, however, the man who first called for postponing the attack at Kursk was Walter Model, commander of the German forces north of the salient.
That winter, Model had “suffered a victory” near the town of Rzhev. The Germans had repelled a Soviet offensive there, but their own losses were too heavy to replace quickly. Now Model, who was supposed to attack the Kursk Arc from the north, wanted more time to prepare and as many reinforcements as he could get. Some other generals argued that the operation should be canceled altogether. Yet the Germans had no alternative plan for the summer of 1943. Trying to hold the entire front through passive defense was a dead end. Sooner or later, the Russians would find a weak spot. In war, it is critical to impose your will on the enemy and make him fight where it suits you.
In the end, the plan was simply revised to accommodate Model’s demands. The delay also gave the Germans time to stockpile ammunition and equip their forces with the latest armored vehicles. The most famous were the heavy Tiger tank, the medium Panther, and the Ferdinand tank destroyer. But the new arsenal included several other models as well, including such exotic machines as the Borgward demolition carrier.
Reinforcements poured into two main strike groups. In the north, Model’s Ninth Army had a fairly straightforward plan: smash through the defenses at a single point with a dense mass of tanks, then drive directly on Kursk. In the south, Manstein devised something more elaborate. Here, the Wehrmacht would attack like a trident. SS panzer divisions advancing toward Kursk through Prokhorovka formed the center prong, but their success depended on two flanking formations. One German panzer corps would advance farther west through Oboyan, while another would creep forward to the east, bypassing Belgorod from that direction. Such a three-pronged breakthrough threatened to trap Soviet forces in a series of encirclements before the Germans even reached Kursk, rapidly collapsing the armies south of the city.
The Germans’ problem was that the Soviets had not been sitting still, meekly awaiting their fate. The plan was too obvious, and intelligence reports confirmed what Soviet commanders had already suspected. As early as April, Marshal Georgy Zhukov outlined the enemy’s most likely course of action. Zhukov was no crystal-ball prophet. All it took to arrive at the broad conclusion was a look at the map and a basic understanding of the enemy’s condition.
Curiously, the Russians received independent confirmation of the coming offensive from intelligence agents operating among their own allies. Kim Philby and John Cairncross of the famous Cambridge spy ring sent Moscow a German radio message intercepted by the British that contained the plan for the operation. Some Soviet commanders favored a preemptive strike. Zhukov and Chief of the General Staff Alexander Vasilevsky, however, decided it would be far wiser to absorb and extinguish the force of the German blow, since they already knew where it would fall.
The Red Army spent the remaining time building defenses around Kursk.
Surrendering the initiative to the enemy is normally extremely risky, but in this case the Russians had a reasonably good idea of where the attack would come. Soviet industry, now operating at full capacity, was supplying the troops with enormous quantities of weapons and materiel. There were also enough men under arms to create not only formidable defensive lines, but a safety cushion in the form of massive reserves.
The Steppe Front was deployed across the base of the salient to provide fresh forces and stabilize the situation if the main line collapsed. A common mistake in discussions of the defense of Kursk, however, is to assume that Soviet commanders cared only about digging trenches, laying mines, and taking other measures designed purely to hold their ground. The reality was far more complex.
While troops facing the German armored fists dug into the earth, Soviet armies were preparing offensives of their own near Orel, north of the Kursk Arc, and in the Donbass to the south. At the decisive moment, those attacks were supposed to force the Germans to abandon their own operations and start plugging holes elsewhere. The Soviet offensives were therefore inseparably linked to the defense of Kursk.
The Russians had to hold out until the Germans were fully committed and had burned through men, machines, supplies, and ammunition. Then the Red Army would strike on other sectors. The offensives near Orel and in the Donbass were expected to force the Germans to halt their attacks around Kursk, while the stubborn defense of the salient would wear them down so badly that they could not stop the new Soviet advances.
In early July, the agonizing wait came to an end.
The North: Ponyri Station and Olkhovatka
Konstantin Rokossovsky commanded the front defending the approaches north of Kursk. He received his final warning from the Stavka on July 2. On the night of July 4-5, a clash erupted in no-man’s-land when Soviet scouts ran into a group of German combat engineers clearing lanes through the minefields. Several Germans were killed and one was captured. The prisoner quickly told his interrogators everything he knew. Acting on his account, Rokossovsky immediately ordered his artillery to begin “counterpreparation” – a preemptive strike against the enemy’s gun batteries. Shelling the German positions before the offensive sounded like a good idea, but Soviet intelligence was inaccurate this time, and the barrage inflicted little damage. The decision was, frankly, a failure. Even so, it was with artillery fire in the predawn gloom that one of the largest battles in world history began.
The Germans may have been expected, but their opening blow still carried tremendous weight. They also deployed technically sophisticated assault formations equipped with Tigers and the latest combat-engineering vehicles. Yet advanced equipment alone could not guarantee a breakthrough. On the first day, Model’s forces pierced the Soviet front in only one sector. To their credit, the Germans had conducted careful, effective reconnaissance and achieved their initial success precisely where they had already identified a weak point.
Even there, however, no easy breakthrough followed. The Wehrmacht ran into minefields of staggering size, covered by artillery and sniper fire. Soviet antitank positions were so well concealed that the Germans usually found them only when the Russians opened fire.
The Germans still had one breach, but Rokossovsky had several reserve rifle divisions and an entire tank army with which to plug it. The constant churn of attack and counterattack disrupted the Germans’ momentum. Even successful Wehrmacht assaults developed slowly, allowing Soviet reserves to arrive and block the advancing units.
After the meager gains of the first few days, Model shifted his main effort toward Ponyri, a station on the railroad running from Orel to Kursk. It was hardly a natural fortress, but after months of preparation the Russians had turned it into a small stronghold ringed, inevitably, by minefields. The backbone of the defense, however, was not the mines. Nearly 20 artillery and antitank regiments and brigades were positioned around the station.
It took the Germans a long time to fight their way toward Ponyri. The defenses there could not win the battle by themselves, but they bought time to determine where the enemy intended to break through and to move reserves into place. Before long, the Germans were concentrating forces wildly out of proportion to the importance of this tiny station and had become trapped in a crude frontal slugfest. As a final argument, they sent in two battalions of their newest equipment: Ferdinand and Brummbär self-propelled guns, both armed with heavy weapons and built to withstand intense fire. On paper, they were a formidable proposition. Heavy assault guns were supposed to blast a path for the infantry deep into the Soviet lines.
In practice, the same thing happened as on the first day. After penetrating a short distance, the Germans found only more minefields and a kill zone covered by a sea of artillery of every conceivable type. The mines forced their vehicles to stop, and stationary armor became prey for the guns. The Ferdinands and Brummbärs were certainly well protected, but shells rained down on them, while the infantry could not follow the armored vehicles because the men had no armor of their own. Deprived of support and stranded before the minefields, the Wehrmacht’s steel battering ram was predictably mauled.
Four artillery regiments fired on the two battalions. Attempting to cross the minefield was deadly even for the heavily armored Ferdinands: conventional mines were interspersed with improvised charges made from aerial bombs and heavy shells. Simply escaping the breach became a problem. The remnants of the German assault units managed to withdraw only by abandoning numerous disabled Ferdinands and several Brummbärs on the battlefield. Rokossovsky later made sure to display these hunting trophies to the press, and Soviet soldiers and officers happily posed for photographers among them. Including tanks and support vehicles, some 35 to 40 machines were left behind in a single field.
Something similar unfolded farther west near Olkhovatka, where German attempts to break through resembled a desperate effort to smash a brick wall with their foreheads. They had to batter not only rifle divisions, but an entire tank army fighting on the defensive. In one final effort, the German corps commander at the spearhead grouped all his tanks into a single division, reinforced it with a Tiger battalion, and tried to punch through a narrow sector with a 200-tank horde. The Germans had some reason for optimism: in the summer of 1943, Soviet armor was markedly inferior in quality.
The legacy of 1942 – when everything capable of moving and firing had been thrown into battle – still made itself felt. Soviet formations contained large numbers of light tanks, still being produced according to the principle of “more of them, for less money,” as well as obsolete Lend-Lease vehicles.
As at Ponyri, artillery became the bedrock of the Soviet defense. The fighting continued largely through inertia, shaving several thousand men a day from the German army while its offensive ground to a complete halt. Model also resisted committing all his forces at once. He expected a Soviet attack on Orel and wanted to retain at least some battleworthy reserves. He would not have to wait long.
The South: Oboyan, Prokhorovka, and the Seversky Donets
South of Kursk, where General Nikolai Vatutin was in command, the situation was much worse. Manstein simply had considerably more forces than Model, and he committed them generously from the very beginning, holding nothing back in reserve. As in the north, the southern “trident” sprang into action on July 5.
The Red Army divided its formations into much smaller units than the Wehrmacht did. A Soviet army was roughly equivalent to a German corps – and was sometimes smaller – while a Red Army corps might be no larger than a second-tier German division. It is hardly surprising, then, that the defenses began to buckle when two German corps slammed into the Soviet Sixth Guards Army.
Even so, the Germans did not have an easy time of it. While the Nazis in the north stalled before the minefields, Manstein’s western prong ran into a colossal antitank ditch. The Russians had “improved” a long, deep, swampy ravine by packing it with explosives, creating an obstacle that held up large German forces. After finally struggling across, they were drawn into savage fighting. For the same reason, the Germans could not use their regiment of brand-new Panthers as a battering ram. They also made an uncharacteristic mistake by failing to provide the Panthers with enough infantry and combat engineers. The result was predictable: one mine explosion after another. The number of Panthers actually destroyed was not spectacular, but the number still fit for combat plunged dramatically and remained between 20 and 50 out of an original 200. Most of the tanks sat forlornly in repair depots.
Meanwhile, however, the SS Panzer Corps found a weak point and, in barely a day, smashed through a defensive line that had taken months to prepare. Here, the Germans not only achieved overwhelming numerical and technical superiority, but put it to effective use. Once again, it must be said that they had conducted painstaking, successful reconnaissance and knew where to strike. At the same time, the episode exposed the inescapable weakness of passive defense: the enemy decides where the main battle will be fought, and you may guess wrong about the location – as defenders usually do.
The front did not collapse west of the German breakthrough. As in the north, a tank army stabilized the situation. This time, the Germans ran into the tankers of General Mikhail Katukov. Facing an assault by hundreds of tanks, Katukov showered the advancing Germans with counterattacks, aided by reinforcements sent from the reserves. The left prong slowed. At the same time, Manstein’s right prong also became bogged down. The positions east of Belgorod along the Seversky Donets River were considered a secondary sector, but the Soviet defenders managed to slow the German tanks there, if not stop them altogether. Vatutin could therefore regard the course of the battle on his eastern and western flanks as more or less satisfactory.
The problem was that, at that very moment, the SS was grinding down the Soviet reserves in the center. The enormous, superbly equipped SS corps advanced like a battering ram, and regiments and brigades arriving from the rear shattered against it like glass. For the time being, the Soviets could not stop the SS.
The glass was half empty, but it was also half full. Every day of the offensive cost the Germans roughly 10% of the armored vehicles committed to the attack. Despite local defeats, Katukov’s tankers and the Soviet infantry had hobbled the German left prong. Even the elite Grossdeutschland Division lost most of its equipment. Soviet high command, however, had no clear picture of the enemy’s condition. More importantly, the SS corps – the knife aimed at the heart of the front – was still moving forward. The Stavka therefore made the quick decision to draw on its safety cushion: the forces of the Steppe Front. The Fifth Guards Tank Army was dispatched from there to meet the SS.
Meanwhile, the II SS Panzer Corps lunged far to the northeast and reached Prokhorovka Station, between the Psel and Seversky Donets rivers. The advance had not been easy.
Counterattacks immediately battered the SS flanks, but something still had to be done about the breakthrough itself – especially since the Germans had already captured the Fifth Guards Tank Army’s intended starting positions for its own counterattack. Units of the SS Leibstandarte Division that had reached Prokhorovka took up defensive positions and prepared to widen the breach toward the Psel. Then, on July 12, the Soviet reserves – the Fifth Guards Tank Army – came crashing down on them.
Unfortunately, the counterattack at Prokhorovka was very poorly prepared. The Fifth Guards Tank Army attacked straight from the march and received nowhere near enough artillery support, let alone air cover. In the rush, there was no time for proper reconnaissance, so the Soviet tankers went in almost blind. Worse still, the same haste meant that the Germans were not struck by an entire tank army advancing in a single formation, but by brigades arriving one after another.
It recalled the ill-fated Soviet counterattacks of the summer of 1941, only in an even worse form. Back then, at least, T-34s and KVs could exploit their powerful armor – by the standards of the time – and close with the enemy. Now the attackers were met by shells from heavily armored German tanks and self-propelled guns that Soviet fire could barely penetrate. Over the course of July 12, the Fifth Guards Tank Army suffered devastating losses while only marginally reducing the SS formations’ ability to continue their advance.
The Germans certainly suffered significant damage: 50 to 70 of their tanks were destroyed or disabled, compared with more than 300 Soviet vehicles. But even the Leibstandarte Division, which absorbed the main blow, remained combat-effective. Strange as it may sound, nothing especially disastrous happened to the Germans at Prokhorovka. In practical terms, the Soviets had merely reset the problem to where it had been before.
Yet the forces of Manstein’s right prong, which had been trying to reach Prokhorovka from the other side, were hobbled and failed to break through. The left prong was bogged down as well. The SS now stood alone deep inside the Soviet defenses, without help or support. And elsewhere, the front was beginning to split at the seams…
The Keys to Kursk
On July 12, as armored armies collided head-on at Prokhorovka, the Soviet Western and Bryansk fronts launched their offensive north of Kursk. Their primary objective was to break through toward Orel. The attack immediately succeeded in several sectors. Walter Model received the news almost with relief. From that point on, there was no longer any question of continuing the northern drive on Kursk.
A Soviet breakthrough toward Orel would carry the Russians directly into the rear of the German forces fighting around Kursk. Model’s immediate superior, Field Marshal Günther von Kluge, did not hesitate for a second. On the first day alone, he dispatched three panzer divisions, one infantry division, and several independent assault-gun brigades to counter the threat. The strike force north of Kursk was dismantled with astonishing speed, almost as though the Germans had been waiting for an excuse. Citadel’s northern pincer had been crossed out with a thick Iron Cross. Rokossovsky’s forces could finally catch their breath: they had held for exactly as long as required.
Orel, however, was not the Nazis’ only problem. On July 10, the Allies had begun landing in Sicily at the opposite end of Europe. That same day, German intelligence detected preparations for a major Soviet offensive in the Donbass, which would indeed begin on July 17. Nor was there much comfort to be found south of Kursk itself. The corps on either side of the SS had been hobbled and could offer no help. The SS corps had broken through and repelled the Soviet counterattacks, but it now sat amid a raging sea of Soviet troops. Continuing the advance offered uncertain benefits, while the Germans risked losing an entire series of battles elsewhere in the meantime. Manstein insisted that, with reinforcements and continued pressure by Model on Rokossovsky, his troops could have reached Kursk. In reality, his argument contained far too many “ifs.”
If Manstein received fresh divisions, if they managed to grind down the Soviet reserves, and if Model resumed his attack, Manstein promised that he could reach Kursk – which still would not have encircled the Soviet armies. Meanwhile, as he fought his way toward the city, the last rites could already be read over the German forces in the Donbass and around Orel. No wonder the Führer passed on that kind of good fortune. Army Group South halted its attacks, and German reserves scattered across the front to plug one gap after another. The Leibstandarte Division was sent to Italy and three more divisions to the Donbass. Operation Citadel had failed completely.
Paradoxically, the Germans were not stopped at the battle’s most famous site – the field at Prokhorovka. On the contrary, it was the only place where the Nazis had achieved success by July 12 and retained the ability to continue their advance. That fact in no way diminishes the courage of the men who counterattacked the SS and died in the armored melee. But the Wehrmacht was stopped primarily by skillful, well-timed operations across the entire front, not by what happened in a single sector.
The Russians had, so to speak, gone over to the offensive at the enemy’s expense. Now they had to make intelligent use of the situation.
The moment of truth
Around Orel, the Russians attacked from three directions: east, northeast, and north. The eastern advance proceeded in fits and starts, but it created a crisis in the German defenses and forced the Wehrmacht to commit reserves. More importantly, those German efforts could do no more than contain it. Northwest of Orel, meanwhile, the situation was turning catastrophic for the Wehrmacht. Ivan Bagramyan’s Eleventh Guards Army quickly broke through the front, and Soviet tank corps poured into the breach. The Germans managed to slow the advance, but within days it became clear that Alexander Gorbatov’s Third Army, driving straight toward Orel from the east, and the Eleventh Guards Army approaching from the north threatened to collapse the German defenses throughout the Orel salient. With the Russians committing a tank army on each axis, the German position became critical.
Contrary to his usual stubbornness, Hitler quickly agreed with his generals that Orel had to be abandoned. The Germans took the breakthrough so seriously that the elite Grossdeutschland Panzer Division – 19,000 men, roughly equivalent to two Soviet tank or mechanized corps – marched around the entire Kursk salient and was transferred from south to north. The Germans managed to slow the Soviet offensive considerably. Soviet commanders would later assess their own performance with striking self-criticism, identifying serious flaws in the operation’s organization. Rokossovsky, who was pressing against the salient from the south at the same time, described it as “pushing” the enemy out rather than destroying him. Even so, it was an unmistakable victory: the Germans were forced to evacuate the Orel salient. The Wehrmacht did withdraw in good order to the fortified Hagen Line at the salient’s base, which the Red Army would have to breach in a separate operation.
Events farther south were even more dramatic.
Vatutin needed time to rebuild his strength and restore order to his front after Manstein’s ferocious offensive. The Russians filled that pause with an attack in the Donbass. Fyodor Tolbukhin’s Southern Front broke through the Wehrmacht defenses along the Mius River and began moving west. The Germans were determined not to surrender the Donbass, a major industrial region, and immediately sent several panzer divisions there. The Russians gave battle. Although the fighting near the village of Stepanovka is far less famous than Prokhorovka, the Germans suffered much heavier losses there, battling Soviet rifle and tank units in sun-drenched cornfields. They managed to push Tolbukhin’s strike force back to its starting positions, only to race straight back toward Belgorod and Kharkov without so much as a pause. The Soviet offensive there began on August 3. The Russians quickly captured Belgorod and drove a wedge into the German defenses north of Kharkov. As at Orel, the Germans tried to stabilize the situation by rapidly maneuvering their panzer divisions. The battle south of Kursk became chaotic, with both sides creating local encirclements and the situation shifting abruptly. On August 23, it culminated in the liberation of Kharkov and the formal end of the Battle of Kursk.
One of the greatest successes of the summer campaign was achieved by what was, on paper, the weakest Soviet force. Tolbukhin’s Southern Front had taken a beating in late July when it failed to break into the Donbass. It was the weakest of the fronts advancing west and had the fewest tanks. But now, with the Germans having withdrawn nearly all their mobile reserves toward Orel and Kharkov, Tolbukhin saw his opportunity. The Russians attacked again almost immediately after losing the first battle on the Mius – and won the second in brilliant fashion. Tolbukhin once more smashed through the front, but this time Manstein could not bury him under panzer divisions. The Russians turned sharply south and pinned a group of several German divisions against the Sea of Azov. The Germans fought their way out of encirclement, abandoning their heavy weapons. Having cleared this mass of enemies from his flank, the Soviet commander wheeled north again and emerged behind the German forces in the Donbass. To escape encirclement, they began a rapid, disorderly retreat from the industrial towns of the steppe. The Donbass, almost impregnable only a short time before, was liberated with remarkable speed and an almost matter-of-fact ease. Hitler raged, but there was nothing he could do. By the end of the first week of September, the Wehrmacht had been driven from the Donbass.
In the wake of these battles, Manstein had to retreat all the way to the Dnieper River. The whole of Army Group South rapidly fell back west toward a line considered strong enough to stop the Red Army’s further advance. The Russians paid dearly for their success. The Wehrmacht remained a highly effective fighting force, and Soviet losses in the battles were approximately twice as high as the Germans’. But the Wehrmacht had lost the strategic initiative. Never again would the Nazis be the active side across the front as a whole. The Russians had liberated a territory the size of a small European country. The German line had lost its stability, and for the next several months the Wehrmacht would be forced to retreat westward, constantly scrambling to patch the holes in its formations.
Kursk is often held up as a model defensive operation. But it is essential to remember that the battle was never simply a matter of sitting behind fixed defenses. The successful defense of Kursk went far beyond digging trenches, laying minefields, and preparing kill zones. It required constant offensive action within the defense, and above all, the preparation of an entire cascade of offensives beyond the Kursk Arc itself. By the time the battle around Kursk reached its climax on the SS corps’ sector, Soviet attacks in other directions had rendered the SS effort pointless – even if it succeeded.
On the Eastern Front, Kursk marked the Wehrmacht’s final strategic offensive. Hard and bloody battles still lay ahead, but no one seriously doubted any longer who would win the war. The German high command still hoped to lock the conflict in a clinch and fight its way to an overall stalemate by clinging to the Dnieper line. Within three months, Berlin would be stripped of that illusion as well.

articles.title: One Russian warehouse smolders near Kazakhstan while a bigger fire rages near St. Petersburg
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones struck a logistics complex belonging to Russian online retailer Ozon in Orenburg on 23 August, the second Ozon warehouse hit in two days, monitoring Telegram channels reported. The site sits about 1,200 km from the war zone, near Russia's border with Kazakhstan. Hours earlier, a large fire tore through a separate warehouse outside St. Petersburg, roughly 900 km north of Ukraine, though local authorities declared no drone or missile threat.
Drones hit Russia's biggest Ozon warehouse
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ published video of the strike moment, after which a fire took hold on the site. Independent Russian outlet Astra analyzed eyewitness footage showing an emergency vehicle racing toward the depot. The complex spans more than 200,000 m² and was designed to hold over 31 million items, ranking among Ozon's biggest in Russia.
The warehouse stands inside the city's special economic zone, a tax-favored industrial park on the eastern edge of European Russia. The first phase opened in August 2024, and a second building followed in 2025.
Orenburg mayor Albert Yumadilov claimed several drones were downed over the special economic zone and that debris fell on the Ozon complex, starting a fire that crews quickly put out with no one hurt.
Ozon confirmed the strike, saying it evacuated more than 300 workers, pulled its goods from the marketplace and stopped taking new deliveries while the site sat idle.
A second fire near St. Petersburg, with no air-raid alert
Overnight, a large blaze hit a warehouse in the Kolpino area south of St. Petersburg. Astra established that the warehouse stood about 350 m from an Ozon site, and witnesses said they heard no drones or air defense. Ukrainian Telegram channel Exile+ identified the burning facility as a storage warehouse run by Logistera.
Part of a widening campaign on Russian marketplace logistics
The Orenburg hit followed the first-ever Ozon strike a day earlier, at a warehouse in Chapaevsk, Samara Oblast. Before turning to Ozon, Ukrainian drones had struck more than 10 warehouses belonging to the larger Russian marketplace Wildberries. Such marketplace hubs move not only consumer goods but dual-use items like electronics and drone components that can reach Russia's military.

articles.title: Ukraine moves to practical work on ballistic missile defense - Zelenskyy spoke about two key projects
articles.body:
Ukraine moves to practical work on ballistic missile defense - Zelenskyy spoke about two key projects
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine is moving from political agreements to practical work on ballistic missile defense. Kyiv is simultaneously developing the pan-European Freyja shield project and producing its own analogues of the missile used by Patriot systems.
Ukraine is moving from political agreements to practical work on its own anti-ballistic capabilities, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Work is underway in two directions at once - the pan-European Freyja anti-ballistic shield and the production of a Ukrainian analogue of missiles for Patriot, reports UNN.
Details
Our anti-ballistic capabilities have several directions. The European direction is our joint Freyja project with Europe, and we are counting heavily on this program. The other direction is Raytheon. We are talking about the possibility of building a Ukrainian missile for the Patriot system. They view this idea positively. They selected a company that can do this - Fire Point. I met with Raytheon in the United States, and we agreed to move forward with this project. After that, they held their first technical meeting with the Ukrainian side regarding the details. Now we will wait for their response. I think we will receive it in the coming weeks. We will get an answer regarding the timeline and an understanding of whether it will succeed or not
In addition, the Freyja project is already moving from political agreements to practical work. European companies are beginning to join the technical implementation of the program directly.
The project has now moved from the leaders' positive reaction and willingness to work to the technical level. Companies are beginning to work in this direction in earnest
Earlier, Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh told UNN that Freyja is at the stage of integrating key components into a single system—radars, a launcher, a command center, and the interceptor missile itself. Testing of individual system components is ongoing.
Russia plans to produce 1,300 ballistic missiles per year
Creating two options at once for Ukraine's anti-ballistic protection, which can be integrated into the European security system, is critically important. After all, as Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, Moscow seeks to reach a ballistic missile production rate of "100 per month," or approximately 1,300 per year. Ukraine has information that Russia currently has accumulated 600–630 ballistic missiles.
Russia could have up to 1,300 ballistic missiles per year. They currently have 600–630. We have an approximate understanding of the level they expect to reach from today through the end of winter. They could have approximately 100 ballistic missiles per month. They do not have that capability yet. We are working to weaken their military industry; there are relevant tasks involving strikes on military targets and other anti-ballistic sanctions
Thus, the third track of anti-ballistic protection for Ukraine is finding 300 missiles for the Patriot system. Obviously, Russia plans to use all those accumulated missiles to strike civilian populations and Ukrainian businesses.
I wanted to find 300 Patriot missiles for the winter package. The request from our Air Force is 360. But when 600 are produced per year, 360 is not easy. We are working with countries on additional possibilities. And I would very much like to believe that we will be able to find a way to obtain some small percentage of the U.S. stockpiles, say 5% or 10%. We are ready to pay for these supplies. In other words, America could replenish its stockpile, and we could get through the winter
We remind you
Fire Point is simultaneously expanding its own production base for missile programs. As the company's CEO Iryna Terekh previously said, at the end of 2027 the company plans to launch a solid rocket fuel plant in Denmark with a total area of more than 120,000 square meters.
The facility will be built in several stages. It is intended to supply fuel for FP-7 missiles, FP-7.x interceptors, and boosters for Flamingo. According to Terekh, locating part of the production capabilities in Denmark makes it possible to create a predictable base protected from Russian strikes for scaling up production.
According to Fire Point's estimate, once it reaches its planned capacity, the plant will be able to produce solid propellant each year for more than 4,100 FP-7 ballistic missiles or FP-7.x ballistic interceptors. During martial law, the company's products are primarily planned to be directed toward Ukraine's needs, while subsequently its production capabilities may also serve the European security system.

articles.title: Iranian artists to showcase works at Sydney exhibition on war and peace
articles.body:
Iranian artists to showcase works at Sydney exhibition on war and peace
TEHRAN- The Benevolent Iranian Women Association will participate in an art exhibition in Sydney, Australia, in early September, presenting selected works by Iranian artists at an event exploring the human consequences of war and destruction.
The association is taking part in the exhibition, titled “When the Earth Embraces the Sky,” at the invitation of Conference of Birds – Shia Hub for Art & Culture of Sydney.
The exhibition, scheduled to run from September 5 to 13, seeks to portray life in Middle Eastern countries before the outbreak of wars and examine the realities faced by people in the aftermath of conflict and destruction.
According to the organizers, the event aims to draw attention to the devastating consequences of war, humanitarian tragedies, war crimes committed in residential areas, and the killing of innocent civilians.
The Iran section of the exhibition will focus on the Minab school massacre as its central theme, highlighting the human cost of attacks that affect civilian and educational spaces.
The Benevolent Iranian Women Association has invited Iranian artists to submit their works for consideration in the exhibition. Artists are requested to send their works to the email address provided in the official announcement or to the email address designated by the association.
The deadline for submissions is September 2, while the exhibition will be held from September 5 to 13.
Cash prizes will also be awarded to three outstanding artworks selected for the exhibition.
On February 28, the Shajareh Tayyebeh girls' elementary school in Minab, Hormozgan province, became the site of a devastating massacre as the United States and Israel initiated their strikes against Iran.
While dozens of girls and boys aged between 7 and 12 were beginning their lessons, the school was targeted by a missile strike that caused the building to collapse, trapping children and teachers beneath the rubble. Iranian authorities confirmed a final death toll of 168 people, with at least 95 others wounded, marking one of the most harrowing incidents of the conflict's opening day.
Despite attempts by US and Israeli authorities to distance themselves from the carnage as images of the tragedy spread across social media, detailed forensic and digital investigations have painted a starkly different picture.
An analysis by Al Jazeera’s digital investigations unit, utilizing over a decade of satellite imagery and recent video clips, revealed that the school was a clearly distinct civilian facility, separated from any adjacent military sites for at least ten years. Furthermore, witness accounts and satellite-based analyses confirmed that the school was triple tapped by three separate, deliberate strikes, leaving no doubt about the nature of the attack.
The international community has faced mounting evidence regarding the responsibility for this atrocity, with investigations from major global outlets including The New York Times, BBC Verify, CBC, and NPR all concluding that the United States was responsible for the strike.
These findings have raised fundamental questions about the intelligence used to justify the bombing, as the patterns of the strike suggest a direct targeting of a civilian educational institution. The Minab school tragedy now stands as a somber testament to the immense human cost of the aggression and a focal point for those demanding international accountability.
SAB/

articles.title: 14 military targets and a second Ozon facility in two days: Ukraine intensifies strikes on Russia
articles.body:
14 military targets and a second Ozon facility in two days: Ukraine intensifies strikes on Russia
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian forces struck 14 Russian military targets, including a Su-33, a MiG-29, an Orion UAV, radars, and an S-400 system. At the same time, the Armed Forces of Ukraine attacked an Ozon logistics hub in Orenburg — the company's second facility in two days.
Ukraine continues to systematically take out Russian aircraft, air defenses, and rear logistics. On August 23, Commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Robert "Madyar" Brovdi published a list of 14 successfully hit military targets, while in Orenburg the Ozon logistics hub came under attack for the second time in two days. Fire Point-produced weapons were used in both operations, UNN reports.
Details
The main part of Madyar's list consists of elements of Russia's air defense. It includes eight radar stations, two surface-to-air missile systems, and an S-400 "Triumf" position.
Thus, of the 14 targets named by Madyar, three were Russian aircraft, while another 11 were part of the enemy's detection and air defense system.
Ozon came under attack for the second time in two days
At the same time, on the morning of August 23, an FP-1 strike drone manufactured by Fire Point hit the logistics complex of the Russian marketplace Ozon in Orenburg. The use of an FP-1 was confirmed to UNN by Fire Point co-owner and chief designer Denys Shtilerman.
For Ozon, this is already the second attack in two days.
On August 22, Ukrainian FP-1 drones hit the company's logistics hub in Chapayevsk, Samara region. The Chapayevsk hub was one of Ozon's largest logistics centers in the Volga region. After all phases were launched, its area amounted to approximately 135,000 square meters, its capacity exceeded 40 million items, and the complex could process more than 215,000 orders per day.
The Ministry of Defense of Ukraine explained the rationale behind the strikes on Russian logistics centers. The ministry emphasized that such facilities are used to store dual-use goods, and that systematically striking them complicates the enemy's logistics and hits the Russian economy.
After the strike on the hub in Chapayevsk, the Ministry of Defense stated that Ukrainian units had previously struck 15 of Wildberries' largest logistics hubs, and that now "it was Ozon's turn."
In fact, these are no longer isolated strikes on individual facilities. Ukraine is simultaneously taking out Russian air defense systems, aircraft, and infrastructure that ensures the movement of goods and supplies within the russian federation.

articles.title: NCSIST releases information on Strong Bow missile
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The National Chung Shan Institute of Science and Technology has released information about its new Strong Bow missile on its website.
The Strong Bow is a land-based, mid-tier system designed to counter tactical ballistic missiles, according to the institute. It can intercept incoming tactical ballistic missiles at medium altitude and form a layered interception network with lower-tier missile defense systems, it added.
The missile uses thrust-vector control during its terminal phase, maintaining excellent maneuverability even in the thin atmosphere, the institute said.
It is equipped with precision guidance and a directional warhead, along with an integrated composite rocket motor that improves manufacturability. Its active electronically scanned array radar supports target classification and identification, engagement of multiple tactical ballistic missile targets, electronic counter-countermeasures, and high-precision tracking.
Each mobile launcher contains four missile canisters.
The military plans to build at least 128 Strong Bow missiles. The system will be deployed alongside Sky Bow III and Patriot Advanced Capability-3 interceptors as part of the layered T-Dome air defense network.

articles.title: Pentagon fires Stars and Stripes chiefs after censorship row
articles.body:
Pentagon fires Stars and Stripes chiefs after censorship row
The Pentagon has fired senior employees of its official newspaper Stars and Stripes after they publicly criticized what they called government interference in its editorial policy.
First published during the US Civil War in 1861, the newspaper has served as a voice for American troops and reaches about 1.4 million readers daily online and through its overseas print editions.
Although partly funded by the Pentagon, it is legally required to maintain editorial independence. The paper recently criticized US tactics in the war against Iran and reported on numerous problems facing the military during the campaign.
Editor-in-chief Erik Slavin, publisher Max Lederer, and Middle East reporter Lara Korte each received a notice of separation on Friday citing insubordination.
Slavin told AP that he was fired “for stating in a CBS interview that hypothetical censorship of news for service members would constitute a red line.”
“I stand by the principle that Stars and Stripes must remain editorially independent, as required by law and by the department’s own policies,” he added.
Korte, who participated in the same interview last month, wrote on X that she was dismissed after telling CBS that she worked for Stars and Stripes and “not the Pentagon, not any administration, and not any policy maker.”
Lederer, who had served as publisher for 19 years and was due to retire in September, wrote in his resignation letter on Tuesday that his understanding of the newspaper’s “value and mission” differed “in fundamental ways” from the Pentagon leadership’s plans.
In an interview published on July 5, the journalists criticized a push to rid the paper of what the Pentagon termed “woke distractions that siphon morale,” as well as changes to regulations guaranteeing its independence. Slavin said his team had been barred from publishing news from paid wire services such as AP, making it “more difficult for us to cover breaking news.”
Jacqueline Smith, the publication’s ombudsman responsible for safeguarding its editorial independence, was fired in January after writing an article critical of Pentagon press restrictions. She later sued the US Department of War, alleging that her dismissal was retaliatory.
Stars and Stripes was among the first outlets to report on deteriorating living conditions and low morale aboard the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, which spent more than 200 days operating near Iran without port calls.
It also reported on ammunition shortages and published an op-ed earlier this month by retired US Army Lieutenant Colonel Daniel L. Davis, who argued that “America’s war against Iran has already been lost at the strategic level.”
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly accused media outlets of spreading “fake news” and sued several of them. War Secretary Pete Hegseth has vowed to push “woke culture” out of the military and revive “the warrior spirit.”

articles.title: Why Trump’s economic pain could spark more Iranian attacks on Gulf nations
articles.body:
Why Trump’s economic pain could spark more Iranian attacks on Gulf nations
The plan is likely to prompt Tehran to retaliate with military strikes across the Gulf in a bid to push up oil prices and force Trump to retreat
President Donald Trump is betting new sanctions, a naval blockade and ramped-up economic pressure against Iran’s trading partners can accomplish what thousands of bombs and missiles could not: force Tehran to accept a deal to end the war on US terms.
But like other US efforts to force Iran into capitulation, there is one main problem: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which has claimed control of the vital Strait of Hormuz and sent volleys of attack drones across the Gulf, may be impervious to such pressure – and has plenty of ways to retaliate.
A major part of the US effort will come on Monday, when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has promised to unveil details of a plan designed to shift the conflict from tit-for-tat strikes across the Middle East to full-blown economic isolation – a campaign that could touch nations ranging from China and India to Turkey and the United Arab Emirates.
Yet significant new economic pressure is likely to prompt Iran to retaliate with military strikes across the Gulf, including against energy infrastructure, in an attempt to push up oil prices and raise the cost of the US effort, forcing Trump to shift his approach once again.
“If this is actually effective, at some point, Iran will lash out again – they just will have no alternative,” said Nate Swanson, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who worked on Iran issues at the State Department and White House National Security Council until last year. “Trump may see this as a different phase of the war, but I don’t think Iran does.”
Since the US and Israel first attacked Iran on February 28, Iran has repeatedly shown the ability to endure air strikes on thousands of targets, layers of sanctions and a US navy blockade – yet still retain the ability to hit back.

articles.title: Russian troops hit Ukrainian army’s energy, transport infrastructure sites in past day
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 23. /TASS/. Russian troops struck fuel and energy and transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian army and enemy deployment sites over the past 24 hours, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"Operational/tactical aircraft, attack unmanned aerial vehicles, missile troops and artillery of the Russian groups of forces struck Ukraine’s fuel and energy and transport infrastructure facilities used by the Ukrainian army, an air defense radar station, workshops assembling and sites storing unmanned aerial vehicles and their components, and also temporary deployment areas of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries in 159 locations," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 1,120 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), eight smart bombs and four US-made HIMARS rockets over the past 24 hours, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported. "Air defense capabilities shot down eight guided aerial bombs, four rockets of the US-made HIMARS multiple launch rocket system and 1,120 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian Battlegroup West forces destroyed Ukraine’s US-made HIMARS multiple rocket launcher during the special military operation over the past day, the Russian Defense Ministry reported on Sunday. "The enemy lost over 210 troops, two armored combat vehicles, 19 motor vehicles, a US-made HIMARS multiple rocket launcher and three artillery guns," the ministry said in a statement.
The Ukrainian army lost roughly 1,355 troops in battles with Russian forces in all the frontline areas over the past 24 hours, according to the latest data on the special military operation in Ukraine released by Russia’s Defense Ministry.
The latest figures show that the Ukrainian army lost roughly 200 troops in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup North, over 210 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup West and more than 225 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup South.
During the last 24-hour period, the Ukrainian army also lost up to 390 troops in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center, more than 305 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup East and roughly 25 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup Dnepr, the latest figures show.

articles.title: Russia planning 'peripheral' mobilization of 300,000 men after elections, Zelensky says
articles.body:
Russia planning 'peripheral' mobilization of 300,000 men after elections, Zelensky says
Russia plans to mobilize around 300,000 people after State Duma elections in September, but will do so without touching the country's major cities in an effort to minimize backlash from society, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky told journalists.
Russia's voluntary recruitment system has increasingly struggled to make up for losses on the battlefield, while diminishing returns in Russian offensives on the front line have fuelled talk of a new wave of mobilization in the country.
Although baring no resemblence to a real democratic process, the Duma Elections are nonetheless seen as a litmus test for support for president Vladimir Putin's regime, and the Kremlin will wait until after to announce a new draft, Zelensky said.
According to Zelensky, the 300,000 mobilized troops will complement existing inflows of recruits into the Russian army, and will either be used to boost Moscow's main offensive effort on the "fortress belt" cities of Donetsk Oblast, or to create new threats in other areas, including Ukraine's northern border.
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow has only once turned to forced mobilization to fill the ranks of its military: in autumn 2022, when successive Ukrainian counteroffensive successes threatened a broader collapse of Russia's defense lines.
The move triggered an exodus of hundreds of thousands of Russians from the country, with long lines at border crossing points, particularly at the state border with Georgia.
Since then, Putin has famously gone to great lengths to avoid more large-scale forced mobilization, seeing it as a threat to his image as provider of strength and stability to ordinary Russians apathetic to questions of politics and war.
Instead, Moscow has relied on lucrative bonuses offered to those who sign a contract, with responsibility resting largely on regional authorities to meet tough recruitment quotas.
According to Zelensky, Putin plans to minimize perceived political consequences by focusing mobilization efforts away from the large population centers, especially Moscow and St Petersburg.
"They are planning for a kind of 'peripheral mobilization,'" the president said.
"As we understand, it won't happen in the central cities. But I don't think they will succeed in hiding it."

articles.title: Turkish sailor killed in second drone strike after rescue – media
articles.body:
Turkish sailor killed in second drone strike after rescue – media
A Turkish sailor who survived a drone attack on one cargo ship was killed when the vessel that rescued him was struck as well, near Russia’s Black Sea coast. Ukraine has been escalating long-range strikes against Russian ports and civilian logistics.
According to multiple Turkish news reports on Saturday, Ilker Lazoglu was the cook on the San Marino-flagged bulker Necibe. The vessel was reportedly struck by drones at Russia’s Black Sea port of Tuapse on Tuesday, where it was scheduled to load 20,000 tons of wheat.
Along with 17 other crew members, he was evacuated to the Ural, a Turkish-owned and Cameroon-flagged vessel, Türkiye Today and Hurriyet reported. However, that ship was reportedly hit near Novorossiysk, which has faced numerous attacks by Ukrainian drones in recent months.
Lazoglu and eight other sailors were injured in the attack, and he later died from his wounds, Hurriyet reported, citing a relative.
For several months, Ukrainian long-range strikes have been targeting Russian ports and international shipping that Kiev suspects of transporting Russian cargoes. Russian officials have warned that Ukraine is “playing with fire” by attacking other countries’ civilian ships in the Black Sea and have condemned the strikes as terrorist acts.
Moscow has retaliated by targeting Ukraine’s key Black Sea ports and shipping it says are handling imports for the Ukrainian military, effectively cutting off the country’s main export route.
Kiev opened this “Pandora’s box” by targeting “civilian targets and logistics,” Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Saturday. Now Ukraine is reaching out via third-party countries to try to prevent the situation from “developing into a catastrophic scenario,” he said, adding that Moscow remains ready for peace talks provided they are based on the realities “on the ground.”

articles.title: The Supreme Court Let Trump’s Ballroom Proceed—for Now. Here’s What That Means
articles.body:
The U.S. Supreme Court has allowed President Donald Trump to continue construction on a new White House ballroom with a temporary stay issued Friday—just before the aboveground portion of the project was about to be halted.
Chief Justice John Roberts, in a one-sentence order, stayed a federal district court judge’s injunction that barred further development. The move gives the full Supreme Court more time to consider the Trump Administration’s request to keep the injunction on hold while it seeks further review. However, there is no established timeline for when Roberts or the Court might take further action.
The ruling comes after months of debate over a legal challenge brought by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which argues that a President cannot unilaterally make a major, permanent change to federally owned property when Congress has not authorized it, pointing toward the Property Clause of the Constitution.
“We reiterated that the Administration has no unilateral legal authority—constitutional, statutory, or otherwise—to build a Ballroom on the site of the now-demolished East Wing, unless and until Congress expressly approves,” the National Trust for Historic Preservation said in a statement last week. “Each court that has reviewed this case has agreed with the National Trust. We hope the Supreme Court will uphold the rule of law by stopping this illegal project.”
Read More: What to Know About Trump’s Aide Natalie Harp
Trump reacted to the administrative stay on Truth Social on Friday, praising both the Supreme Court and Roberts, who was appointed by former President George W. Bush in 2005.
“We are grateful for the Decision of the United States Supreme Court,” Trump said. “The Military/Ballroom Complex being built on the hallowed grounds of the White House, which is so vital for National Security, will be THE GREATEST OF ITS KIND!”
Here’s what to know about the latest updates on the $400 million project.
How did the ballroom case reach the Supreme Court?
Two lower-court decisions brought the dispute before the Supreme Court.
First, Senior Judge Richard Leon of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia found that the National Trust was likely to succeed on its claim that the project required congressional approval, and he ruled in March that construction on the aboveground ballroom could not take place while litigation continued. He modified that preliminary injunction on April 16 to clarify that security-related work could continue if it is "strictly necessary to ensure the safety and security of the White House.”
The second decision came when the Trump Administration appealed, and a D.C. Circuit panel upheld the modified injunction. In its August ruling, it said that each President is a “temporary tenant, not the owner,” of the White House.
According to Kimberly Wehle, professor of law at the University of Baltimore School of Law, the injunction is meant to ensure that the project does not advance while the courts review its legality, the limits of presidential authority, and whether it might cause irreparable harm.
“The court is saying, ‘We just need to stop the bleeding right now, because if this continues, it'll just cause more harm,’” she tells TIME.
The Trump Administration then asked the Supreme Court to intervene through an emergency application, which is meant for urgent review of time-sensitive matters that fall outside of the typically months- or years-long case review timeline for the country’s highest court.
The case was put in front of Roberts, who oversees emergency appeals filed in the D.C. Circuit.
That led to the administrative stay—a short-term order that freezes a lower court decision or deadline in order to buy time for a bench to review an emergency request. An administrative stay does not reflect a case’s merits or legality; it acts as an interim measure for a future ruling from Roberts or the Court.
In this case, it paused the preliminary injunction originally handed down by Leon. Therefore, the stop-work order was put aside for the time being, allowing construction to continue.
"We are aware of the administrative stay," the National Trust tells TIME, in response to the latest developments. "To be clear, this is not a final decision on the merits of the government’s stay application, and we await further action.”
No court has issued a final ruling on the project’s legality. But next steps will likely include determining whether the renovation is two distinct projects—aboveground and below—or a singular build.
Is Trump building a ballroom or a military complex?
Trump’s 90,000-square-foot construction project comprises a luxury ballroom—which is meant to host 650 seated guests—with an underground military complex beneath it, featuring “protective missile resistant steel columns, beams, drone proof roofing materials, and bullet, ballistic, and blast proof glass,” according to one court document.
Lower courts treated the two components separately, finding that the National Trust was likely to establish that the aboveground ballroom required congressional approval while exempting underground security construction from the injunction.
In making his injunction determination, Leon said: “Defendants themselves distinguished between below-ground and above-ground construction, stating that ‘the below-surface work is driven by national security concerns independent of the above-grade construction.’”
Leon and the D.C. Circuit said the Administration had shifted from treating the components as independent to describing them as inseparable. The Administration disputes that characterization, saying the design became less flexible as construction progressed. It now argues that the entire project is integrated and that halting the aboveground work would compromise its structural integrity and security functions.
“Every day the President does not have access to the vital security features of the military complex presents unacceptable risk, no matter how long the Project takes to complete,” Solicitor General John Sauer argued in court filings last week. “Built with integrated engineering, the Project will provide in a very large way, a ‘safe room’ for the Presidency and the continuity of government.”
Presidents in the past have relied on the White House’s Presidential Emergency Operations Center (PEOC), which dates to World War II, as a safe room or bunker. The Administration has argued that the former East Wing’s security infrastructure had become vulnerable to modern threats, including drones and missiles, making the new construction urgent.
In court documents, it claimed the former building “cannot protect guests against inclement weather, let alone high-powered weapons.”
The White House in August shared AI-generated images of drones, military personnel, and vehicles on the roof of the ballroom. Trump has claimed that a “drone port” will feature a launching deck and defense station.
He told reporters in March on Air Force One that the ballroom would become a “shed for what’s being built under” and that it would have its own security features, such as bulletproof glass.
Whether or not the two components are accepted as a single entity, from a legal standpoint, could determine the outcome of the outstanding emergency relief.
Could construction outrun judicial review?
In Trump’s post on social media Friday, he said that construction of the ballroom “is under budget and ahead of schedule.”
The Administration claimed in its Aug. 13 application that 65% of construction was done. When the project was announced in 2025, the White House said that construction would be done “long before the end of President Trump’s term.” The Administration is now saying that the framework will be substantially complete by November, with the official completion date set for August 2028, according to appendixes to the emergency application that was submitted by the Trump Administration.
This raises the question of whether a majority of the structure could be completed before the litigation is resolved.
Lawyers for the National Trust accused the Trump Administration in a court filing earlier this month of “trying to outrun judicial review,” pointing to the Administration’s own assertion that the structure will soon be “virtually impossible to deconstruct.”
Wehle says that Roberts’s stay is “giving Trump exactly what he wants” by allowing him to get ever closer to the project’s completion while the courts assess whether he is breaking the law.
“This is the Supreme Court greenlighting unconstitutional, lawless behavior by the President,” Wehle says. She questions whether the President is being accommodated because it seemed like the project had gone too far and might be harder to undo at this point than to simply finish—especially when weighing the potential harm to the public in terms of cost, damage, and timeline.
But if that’s true, she asks, “What kind of precedent does that set?”
“That is a precedent that says the law is optional,” she explains. That could embolden a strategy of acting first and asking permission second, if at all.
If the project were ultimately found unlawful after construction was substantially or entirely complete, the case could present unusual questions about what remedy remained available—including whether a court could order the structure altered, reverted, or removed.

articles.title: Over the past 24 hours, the Ukrainian Armed Forces eliminated 1,310 Russians on the front and destroyed 26 armored vehicles
articles.body:
Over the past 24 hours, the Ukrainian Armed Forces eliminated 1,310 Russians on the front and destroyed 26 armored vehicles
Kyiv • UNN
The total losses of the Russian army have reached 1,476,580 troops. Over the past day, 1,310 occupiers, 26 armored vehicles, and 1,925 drones were destroyed.
As of August 23, 2026, the total combat losses of Russian forces in the war against Ukraine amount to approximately 1,476,580 personnel, while over the past day Ukrainian troops eliminated another 1,310 occupiers, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported, UNN writes.
Details
According to the General Staff, since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, the Russian army has also lost 12,292 tanks and 25,202 armored combat vehicles. Over the past day, the number of destroyed armored vehicles increased by 26, while no tank losses were recorded.
Russian artillery losses amount to 48,451 systems, 69 of which were destroyed over the past day. Ukrainian troops also destroyed one air defense system, bringing the total number of such losses to 1,585 units.
Aviation and drone losses
According to the General Staff, Russian forces have lost 440 aircraft and 354 helicopters. One aircraft was destroyed over the past day.
The General Staff separately reported 476,566 destroyed operational-tactical unmanned aerial vehicles. Over the past day, Ukrainian troops destroyed another 1,925 such UAVs. In addition, the total losses of Russian forces amount to 2,352 ground robotic systems, eight of which were destroyed over the past day.
The largest losses by number remain those of motor vehicles and fuel tankers — 138,219 units. Over the past day, Ukrainian troops destroyed another 415 units of such equipment. Total losses of special-purpose equipment amount to 4,569 units, four of which were destroyed over the past day.

articles.title: Finland to Manufacture Drones for Ukraine and Europe
articles.body:
Ukrainian and Finnish companies have signed agreements to develop and manufacture drones in Finland to supply both the Ukrainian military and European markets.
President Volodymyr Zelensky announced the agreements on Sunday, Aug. 23, following a roundtable meeting in Kyiv with Finnish President Alexander Stubb focused on defense-industrial cooperation.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Today we are taking another step toward deepening our cooperation, combining Ukrainian combat experience with Finnish technologies,” Zelensky wrote on Facebook.
According to the president, the newly signed documents cover the joint production of uncrewed aerial vehicles, the expansion of capabilities in maritime uncrewed systems, and the establishment of a joint venture dedicated to producing ground robotic complexes.
Zelensky emphasized the timing of the agreement, which coincides with Ukraine’s National Flag Day and the eve of its Independence Day.
“On these important dates, we especially feel the value of true friendship,” he stated, expressing gratitude to Stubb, the Finnish government, businesses, and the people of Finland for their steadfast support since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Expanding the Drone Deal format
The agreements with Finland follow a broader diplomatic push by Kyiv to secure long-term defense cooperation pacts under what it calls the “Drone Deal” format.
On July 7, during the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, Ukraine signed similar Drone Deal agreements with Estonia and the Netherlands.
UN Security Council to Discuss Ukraine on Independence Day
At the time, Zelensky described the agreements as “full-fledged” cooperation deals covering joint drone production, technology development, and systematic arms exports.
During that same summit, Zelensky and Stubb held a separate meeting to discuss the timelines and terms for finalizing their own bilateral Drone Deal.
The overarching initiative aims to scale up international defense manufacturing, utilizing Ukrainian combat-tested expertise while mitigating the risk of Russian strikes on domestic production facilities by relocating joint ventures to allied nations.

articles.body:
- Category

Ukraine’s Armed Robot Rolls Into Russian Position and Opens Fire, Killing 20, Video
Ukrainian troops used an armed unmanned ground vehicle to attack a Russian-held position without sending soldiers into direct-fire range, killing 20 Russian troops, according to Ukrainian defense technology company DevDroid.
Soldiers from Ukraine’s 44th Separate Mechanized Brigade carried out the operation using the company’s Droid TW-12.7 strike UGV, DevDroid said in an August 21 press release.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian troops had taken shelter inside a building at one of their positions, according to the company. Ukrainian operators remotely drove the ground robot toward the structure before opening fire with its remotely controlled combat module armed with a 12.7 mm (.50-caliber) M2 Browning heavy machine gun.
DevDroid said the position was neutralized and 20 Russian troops were killed during the engagement. The casualty figure could not be independently verified.
The entire attack was conducted remotely.
Instead of Ukrainian infantry having to approach the Russian position under fire, the Droid TW-12.7 performed the most dangerous part of the mission itself—closing the distance to the target and engaging the troops inside with direct machine-gun fire.
Developed by Ukrainian engineers at DevDroid, the Droid TW-12.7 was designed as a combined reconnaissance and strike platform capable of operating close to frontline positions.
Its remotely operated weapons system is paired with onboard cameras, a ballistic computer and AI-assisted functions designed to help operators detect, track and engage targets while remaining away from the immediate combat zone.
The vehicle’s M2 Browning gives it substantial firepower for a relatively compact unmanned platform. The heavy machine gun can be used against infantry, firing positions, unarmored vehicles and some lightly armored targets.
The Droid can also provide remote battlefield surveillance, transmitting video and other data to its operators in real time and allowing Ukrainian troops to observe hostile positions without physically moving into exposed areas.
That combination allows the platform to support both offensive and defensive missions—from reconnaissance and fire support to direct attacks on fortified positions in areas where sending troops forward could carry a high risk of casualties.
The Droid TW-12.7 is built for mobility across rough terrain and off-road conditions and has already been tested in combat environments.
Previously, an armed Ukrainian ground robot was carried across the water by an uncrewed maritime platform, landed on the Russian-held Kinburn Spit, and sent into combat—an operation the military described as the first known mission of its kind anywhere in the world.

articles.title: Zelensky: Ukraine Strikes Russian Iskander Launcher
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck a Russian Iskander-M missile launcher in Russia.
The Ukrinform news agency reported this, citing a statement by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky during a conversation with journalists.
“Today we have another success. We cannot provide many details due to the sensitivity of the operation, but the fact is the fact. We struck an Iskander launcher near our borders. I am grateful to our soldiers who are carrying this out. This is our operation to hunt their systems located nearby,” he said.
According to the president, striking launchers in Russia’s border regions is one way of countering Russian missile attacks.
“In other words, this is one of the ways when our anti-ballistic missiles are limited — there is another tactic, which is more difficult, that we have developed. It is hunting their nearby launch sites from which they launch ballistic missiles. This is a separate matter, a separate program, a separate operation,” Zelensky added.
At the same time, Zelensky said that SpaceX ultimately refused to allow Ukraine to use Starlink in Russia due to the risk of escalation.
According to Zelensky, in the first half of 2026, the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine asked him to negotiate with U.S. President Donald Trump over the use of Starlink in Russia for Ukraine’s defense needs, as SpaceX and its CEO, Elon Musk, had allegedly already agreed to such a possibility, but it required political approval.
During a meeting with Trump, Zelensky raised the issue and argued that using Starlink would help limit Russia’s ability to prolong the war and bring it closer to an end.
Trump said he would consider Ukraine’s request and discuss it with Musk, but made no commitments to a positive decision.
During a subsequent meeting with Zelensky, Trump said SpaceX had refused Ukraine’s request to use Starlink in Russia due to the risk of escalation.
Volodymyr Zelensky stressed that Ukraine continues to discuss the issue with Trump and the U.S. side.
“Today, all of this is on the U.S. president’s side, and they are already having their own internal discussions,” Zelensky said.
